findings.title: `sizedview` property docstring claims `.<field>` always returns a BoundField, but nested-Struct fields return a _SizedView and Array fields raise
findings.description: The public `sizedview` property docstring states unconditionally that `t.sizedview.<field>` returns a BoundField. In fact _SizedView.__getattr__ (lines 1221-1230) returns the child's own `.sizedview` (a _SizedView, not a BoundField) for a nested-Struct field, and raises AttributeError for an Array field. So the blanket claim is wrong for two of the three field kinds. The internal _SizedView docstring gets this right, but the user-facing property docstring does not, and `<field>` reads as a universal placeholder.
findings.evidence: property docstring (lines 850-851): "``t.sizedview.<field>`` returns a :class:`BoundField` -- a live lvalue\n        handle."  --- vs code (lines 1221-1229): `if isinstance(ftype, StructMeta): return getattr(owner, name).sizedview` and `if isinstance(ftype, Array): ... raise AttributeError(...)`.
findings.suggestion: Qualify the claim, e.g. 'For a scalar field, `t.sizedview.<field>` returns a BoundField; a nested-Struct field returns the child's own sizedview, and an array field raises (access its live list via the field directly).'
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and verified. The public `sizedview` property docstring (bytemaker/structs.py:850-851) states unconditionally: "``t.sizedview.<field>`` returns a :class:`BoundField` — a live lvalue handle." But `_SizedView.__getattr__` (lines 1221-1230) branches: a nested-Struct field (`isinstance(ftype, StructMeta)`) returns `getattr(owner, name).sizedview` (a `_SizedView`, not a `BoundField`), and an Array field (`isinstance(ftype, Array)`) raises `AttributeError`; only the scalar fall-through (line 1230) returns `BoundField`. So the blanket claim, with `<field>` reading as a universal placeholder, is wrong for two of three field kinds. The internal `_SizedView` docstring (line 1206) correctly notes "nested-Struct fields return the child's own sizedview," confirming the author knew the nuance and just didn't carry it into the user-facing property docstring. This is a real, evidence-backed doc gap on a public API, not a nitpick and not the intentional narrative style. I downgrade severity from medium to low: it is an over-generalized omission (two cases missing) rather than an actively false claim on the primary documented path — the scalar lvalue semantics the docstring describes are correct — and one of the two omitted cases (Array) does at least raise a self-explanatory error. Confidence stays high; the discrepancy is unambiguous in the code.

findings.title: `array()` docstring 'Sugar for `field(element * count)`' omits the endian parameter the function actually accepts
findings.description: array() has signature `array(element, count, *, endian=None, default=_MISSING)` and builds `Array.of(element, count, endian)`. Its docstring describes it only as 'Sugar for `field(element * count)`', but `element * count` resolves to `Array.of(element, count)` with no endian (see BitTypeMeta.__mul__ at bittype.py:74 and Array.__mul__ at structs.py:1509, neither of which takes endian). The docstring never mentions the `endian` (or `default`) keyword, so a reader cannot tell array() can set per-array byte order -- the one thing it offers over the `field(element * count)` spelling it claims full equivalence to.
findings.evidence: docstring (lines 655-656): "Declare a fixed-count array field: ``colors: list[int] = array(UInt16, 8)``.\n    Sugar for ``field(element * count)`` with a plain-list checker type."  --- vs signature (lines 648-654) which includes `endian: Any = None` and passes it through: `return _FieldSpec(Array.of(element, count, endian), default)`.
findings.suggestion: Add a sentence documenting the `endian` keyword (and note `default`), or soften the 'sugar for field(element * count)' claim to note array() additionally lets you set the array's byte order and a default.
findings.verifyReason: Verified accurate against current code. bytemaker/structs.py:648-657: array(element, count, *, endian=None, default=_MISSING) forwards endian into Array.of(element, count, endian). Its docstring (lines 655-656) says only "Sugar for ``field(element * count)``". But element * count resolves to Array.of(..., count) with NO endian in both BitTypeMeta.__mul__ (bittype.py:74-77) and Array.__mul__ (structs.py:1509-1510) — confirmed Array.of takes endian at structs.py:1356-1361. So array()'s two distinguishing keywords, endian (per-array byte order) and default, are exactly what it offers over the `field(element * count)` spelling it claims equivalence to, yet neither is mentioned. This is a genuine documentation-completeness gap on a public API function (array is a dataclass_transform field_specifier). Not a nitpick and not the intentional narrative-style; it is a "sugar for X" claim that understates the function. Severity is low: the docstring does not break anything or actively mislead into wrong behavior — endian is visible in the signature and documented elsewhere (BitTypeMeta docstring at bittype.py:69-72 explains picking byte order via Array.of). Confidence raised to high because every load-bearing fact was directly read and confirmed. Suggested fix (soften the "sugar for" claim or add a sentence documenting endian/default) is apt.

findings.title: .pyi docstring says float boxes satisfy SupportsIndex, but Float has no __index__
findings.description: The stub's module docstring covers all three alias kinds (it names int/float reads) and states that write/__init__ values may be 'BitType boxes (which satisfy SupportsIndex via Int.__index__).' That is only true for the integer aliases. The very same stub declares `_FloatAlias.__set__(self, obj, value: SupportsFloat | SupportsIndex)` (line 26), i.e. a float field accepts a box via SupportsFloat. A boxed Float has __float__ but NO __index__ (bittypes/float.py defines __float__ at line 67; there is no __index__ on Float or its bases), so a Float box does NOT satisfy SupportsIndex. The docstring omits the SupportsFloat/__float__ channel that the stub itself encodes, misdescribing how float fields accept boxes.
findings.evidence: Docstring: "reads are plain int/float, writes and the synthesized __init__ parameters accept anything the narrowing store accepts - plain ints and, post-D2, BitType boxes (which satisfy SupportsIndex via Int.__index__)."  vs the stub it documents: `class _FloatAlias: ... def __set__(self, obj: Any, value: SupportsFloat | SupportsIndex) -> None: ...`  (Float in bittypes/float.py has `def __float__` but no `__index__`.)
findings.suggestion: Mention both channels, e.g. '... BitType boxes: integer boxes via SupportsIndex (Int.__index__), float boxes via SupportsFloat (Float.__float__)', matching the _FloatAlias.__set__ signature.
findings.verifyReason: Accurate and verified. The .pyi module docstring (bytemaker/fields.pyi:4-7) states writes/__init__ accept "BitType boxes (which satisfy SupportsIndex via Int.__index__)" as the sole box-acceptance mechanism, while covering all three alias kinds ("reads are plain int/float", line 5). That mechanism is int-only. Confirmed: Int defines __index__ (bittypes/int.py:62); Float defines __float__ (bittypes/float.py:67) and has NO __index__ — grep for __index__ across bittypes/ hits only int.py, and Float extends BitType[float] directly (float.py:22), not Int, and BitType itself defines neither. The same stub declares _FloatAlias.__set__(self, value: SupportsFloat | SupportsIndex) (line 26), and the runtime float field store uses float(value), i.e. the SupportsFloat/__float__ channel (structs.py:217), not operator.index(). So the docstring omits the very channel the stub encodes and the runtime uses for float boxes — a genuine internal contradiction, not the intentional narrative style. Not a nitpick: it misdescribes how float fields accept boxes and contradicts the adjacent signature. Downgraded medium->low because this is an annotation-only stub docstring: the _FloatAlias.__set__ signature is itself correct, so type checkers behave correctly and there is no runtime/user-facing breakage; the mislead is confined to a human reading the stub docstring. The suggested one-line fix (name both channels) is apt. Confidence high — every load-bearing claim independently verified.

findings.title: __init__ buffer docstring drifts from __new__ on copy-vs-share (native backend)
findings.description: The native backend's __new__ docstring is careful to state that `buffer=` copies on this reference backend ('this reference backend copies', lines 176-178). The __init__ docstring for the same param just says 'the BitVector's bits are read from the provided buffer object' with no copy note, so a reader of __init__ alone gets the may-share impression the __new__ docstring deliberately corrects. bitvector_speedup.py avoids this by having __init__ defer entirely to __new__ ('See __new__ for construction semantics').

findings.verifyReason: Verified all three cited passages verbatim. This is a genuine, accurate inter-backend documentation inconsistency, not a flag of the intentional narrative style and not a lie (it omits rather than contradicts). Low severity is correct: no reader is pushed toward a wrong action, and this backend always copies. Confidence held at medium because it is a minor polish item on a redundant docstring rather than a load-bearing correctness issue.
